title: What fall protection training does OSHA require in construction?
description: What 29 CFR 1926.503 requires: a fall protection training program, a competent person trainer, a written certification record and three retraining triggers.
shortAnswer: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) requires construction employers, under 29 CFR 1926.503, to provide a training program for each employee who might be exposed to fall hazards, delivered by a competent person and covering eight listed topics. The employer must prepare a written certification record with the employee's name, training dates and a signature, keep the latest certification, and retrain when changes or observed gaps make previous training inadequate.
keyTakeaways: 1926.503(a)(1) covers "each employee who might be exposed to fall hazards", which in construction generally means work 6 feet or more above a lower level under 1926.501.
Training must be given by a competent person qualified in eight areas listed in 1926.503(a)(2), from the nature of fall hazards to the standards in Subpart M.
The written certification record must show the employee's name or identity, the training date(s) and the signature of the trainer or employer, and only the latest certification has to be kept.
Retraining is required when workplace changes, changes in fall protection systems, or gaps in an employee's knowledge make earlier training inadequate. There is no fixed refresher interval.
Fall protection training (1926.503) was eighth, and the underlying duty to have fall protection (1926.501) first, in federal OSHA's preliminary most cited standards for fiscal year 2026.
jurisdiction: United States (federal, with OSHA-approved State Plans)
regulator: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), US Department of Labor
appliesTo: Construction employers whose employees might be exposed to fall hazards covered by 29 CFR 1926 Subpart M
Roofers, ironworkers, framers, concrete and leading edge workers, and other trades working at height
Employees acting as safety monitors or working under a fall protection plan
Competent persons who deliver fall protection training

sections.heading: Who needs fall protection training under 1926.503?

blocks.text: Every construction employee who might be exposed to fall hazards needs it. Paragraph (a)(1) of [29 CFR 1926.503](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1926.503) says "The employer shall provide a training program for each employee who might be exposed to fall hazards," and that the program must enable each employee to recognize the hazards of falling and train them in procedures to minimize those hazards.

The word "might" matters. The duty is triggered by potential exposure, not by whether fall protection is currently in use. In practice the trigger follows [29 CFR 1926.501](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1926.501), which requires protection for each employee on a walking or working surface with an unprotected side or edge 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level. OSHA's [fall protection overview](https://www.osha.gov/fall-protection) confirms the construction threshold is 6 feet, compared with four feet in general industry, five feet in shipyards and eight feet in longshoring.

Section 1926.503 says it "supplement[s] and clarif[ies]" the general construction training duty in 1926.21, which requires employers to instruct each employee in recognizing and avoiding unsafe conditions. That general duty is covered on the [OSHA training requirements](/regulations/osha-training-requirements) page; this page covers what Subpart M adds.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects 29 CFR 1926.501 and 1926.503 and OSHA guidance as at November 2026. Scaffold work is governed by its own training section, 1926.454, covered on the [OSHA scaffold training](/regulations/osha-scaffold-training-requirements) page. State Plan states may adopt different or additional fall protection rules.

sections.heading: What must the training program cover?

blocks.text: It must cover eight areas, and the trainer must be a competent person qualified in them. Paragraph (a)(2) requires the employer to "assure that each employee has been trained, as necessary, by a competent person qualified in the following areas":

items: the nature of fall hazards in the work area
the correct procedures for erecting, maintaining, disassembling and inspecting the fall protection systems to be used
the use and operation of guardrail systems, personal fall arrest systems, safety net systems, warning line systems, safety monitoring systems, controlled access zones and other protection to be used
the role of each employee in the safety monitoring system when this system is used
the limitations on the use of mechanical equipment during roofing work on low-sloped roofs
the correct procedures for handling and storage of equipment and materials and the erection of overhead protection
the role of employees in fall protection plans
the standards contained in Subpart M

blocks.text: The phrase "as necessary" lets the employer tailor content. A crew that never uses safety nets or works on low-sloped roofs does not need items 4 and 5 in depth, but the employer should be able to explain why each topic was included or left out for each crew. Items 1 and 2 relate to "the work area" and "the fall protection systems to be used", so they cannot be fully covered by a generic course.

sections.heading: Who is allowed to deliver fall protection training?

blocks.text: A competent person qualified in the listed areas. OSHA's construction definitions in [29 CFR 1926.32](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1926.32) describe a competent person as "one who is capable of identifying existing and predictable hazards in the surroundings or working conditions which are unsanitary, hazardous, or dangerous to employees, and who has authorization to take prompt corrective measures to eliminate them."

The standard does not require a particular certificate or course for the trainer. What matters is the combination of hazard recognition ability, knowledge of the specific systems being taught, and authority to act. An external trainer can deliver the program, but the employer still certifies it and remains responsible for site specific content.

sections.heading: What must the written certification record contain?

blocks.text: It must contain the employee's name or other identity, the date or dates of training, and the signature of the trainer or the employer. Paragraph (b)(1) says the employer "shall verify compliance with paragraph (a) of this section by preparing a written certification record." Paragraph (b)(2) adds: "The latest training certification shall be maintained."

There is one less obvious rule. If the employer relies on training given by another employer, or completed before the section took effect, the record "shall indicate the date the employer determined the prior training was adequate rather than the date of actual training." A new hire's card from a previous employer is therefore not enough by itself: the hiring employer has to assess the training and record the date of that determination.

Only the latest certification must be kept, which is less than many employers keep by policy. Keeping superseded records can still help show a pattern of retraining. See [how long to keep training records](/guides/how-long-to-keep-training-records) for retention approaches.

sections.heading: When is fall protection retraining required?

blocks.text: Whenever the employer has reason to believe a trained employee no longer has the required understanding and skill. Paragraph (c) requires retraining in that situation and lists three circumstances that are included but not exhaustive:

items: changes in the workplace render previous training obsolete
changes in the types of fall protection systems or equipment to be used render previous training obsolete
inadequacies in an affected employee's knowledge or use of fall protection systems or equipment indicate that the employee has not retained the requisite understanding or skill

blocks.text: There is no annual requirement in 1926.503. Retraining is driven by events, so the useful control is a set of triggers that supervisors act on: a new site type, a switch from guardrails to personal fall arrest, a new anchor or lifeline system, or an observed misuse. Each trigger should generate a retraining record and an updated certification. For designing event based and periodic refresh rules together, see [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

sections.heading: How often is fall protection training cited?

blocks.text: Often enough to appear in OSHA's top 10 most cited standards. OSHA's [preliminary top 10 list](https://www.osha.gov/top10citedstandards) for fiscal year 2026 (October 1, 2025 to August 31, 2026) places fall protection general requirements (1926.501) first and fall protection training (1926.503) eighth across all industries. A missing or incomplete certification record is a straightforward citation because paragraph (b) prescribes exactly what the record must show.

sections.heading: How can a contractor map 1926.503 to roles and evidence?

blocks.text: Map each paragraph (a)(2) topic to the roles that need it, the trigger, and evidence that shows the person can apply it. The table below is an original, illustrative mapping. It complements a [verification of competency](/glossary/verification-of-competency) approach in which a supervisor observes the skill rather than relying on attendance alone.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models the Subpart M training topics, systems and roles as a framework first, then attaches observed skill checks and knowledge items to each topic. When a crew moves to a new system or site type, the framework shows which topics need retraining and which certifications must be reissued.

faqs.q: Is a fall protection card from a previous employer valid?
faqs.a: It can be used, but the new employer must decide whether the earlier training is adequate for its own work area and systems. Under 1926.503(b)(1), the certification record must then show the date the employer made that determination, not the original training date. If the systems differ, retraining on those systems is required.

faqs.q: Does OSHA require annual fall protection training?
faqs.a: No. 1926.503 sets no fixed interval. It requires retraining when changes in the workplace or fall protection systems make previous training obsolete, or when an employee's knowledge or use shows they have not retained the necessary skill. Many contractors adopt a periodic refresher as policy in addition to these triggers.

Online content can support the knowledge portion, but the standard requires training by a competent person in the procedures and systems to be used in the work area, including erecting, inspecting and using equipment. Those elements generally need hands-on instruction and observation, which online delivery alone does not provide.

Scaffolds have their own training section, 1926.454, and their own fall protection trigger of more than 10 feet in 1926.451(g)(1). An employee who works both on scaffolds and on other elevated surfaces may need training under both sections.
